  2279  IV. Section-by-Section Analysis
  2280  
  2281      In this section, OPM discusses the regulatory amendments to 5 CFR 
  2282  chapter I, subchapter B, part 351, subpart I, governing appeals of and 
  2283  corrective action with respect to RIFs.
  2284  
  2285  A. Section 351.802--Content of Notice
  2286  
  2287      OPM is revising Sec.  351.802(a)(6), which governs the information 
  2288  an agency must include in a written notice to an employee affected by a 
  2289  reduction in force. Current Sec.  351.802(a)(6) refers to the 
  2290  employee's right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board. 
  2291  Because this final rule transfers adjudication of covered RIF appeals 
  2292  from MSPB to OPM, revised Sec.  351.802(a)(6) replaces the MSPB 
  2293  reference with a reference to OPM.
  2294      The revised provision requires an agency's RIF notice to inform the 
  2295  employee, as applicable, of the employee's right to appeal to OPM. As 
  2296  revised in this final rule, the notice must also state the time limit 
  2297  for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and identify the electronic 
  2298  filing system, available on OPM's website, through which an appeal must 
  2299  be filed. This requirement preserves the practical filing information 
  2300  previously conveyed through the cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 of 
  2301  this title and forecloses any contention that a RIF notice failed to 
  2302  apprise an employee of how and when to appeal. The provision is 
  2303  conforming in nature and is intended to ensure that employees receive 
  2304  accurate notice of the administrative appeal forum established by 
  2305  revised subpart I. The revision does not eliminate any independently 
  2306  applicable statutory notice requirement or any separately available 
  2307  remedial process administered by another entity.
  2308      The proposed rule retained legacy language in Sec.  351.802(a)(6) 
  2309  requiring agencies to comply with Sec.  1201.21 of this title, as 
  2310  applicable. OPM is removing that cross-reference in the final rule. 
  2311  Section 1201.21 is an MSPB notice provision that applies when an agency 
  2312  issues a decision notice in a matter appealable to the Board. It 
  2313  requires MSPB-specific information, including notice of the time limits 
  2314  for appealing to the Board, the address of the appropriate Board 
  2315  office, access to the Board's regulations, and access to the MSPB 
  2316  appeal form. Because this final rule replaces MSPB with OPM as the 
  2317  adjudicative forum for RIF appeals under part 351, retaining an 
  2318  unqualified cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 in the RIF notice 
  2319  provision could create confusion about where an affected employee must 
  2320  file a RIF appeal.
  2321  
  2322  [[Page 49248]]
  2323  
  2324      This deletion is conforming, clarifying, and nonsubstantive. It 
  2325  does not eliminate any appeal right, shorten any filing period, alter 
  2326  the information an agency must provide about the OPM RIF appeal right, 
  2327  or affect any matter that remains independently appealable to MSPB. 
  2328  Rather, it removes an obsolete MSPB-specific notice cross-reference 
  2329  from a provision that now concerns OPM RIF appeals. To the extent an 
  2330  employee has an independent statutory or regulatory right to proceed 
  2331  before MSPB on a collateral matter, that right remains governed by the 
  2332  statutes and regulations applicable to that matter consistent with 
  2333  Sec.  351.901(c).
  2334  
  2335  B. Section 351.807--Certification of Expected Separation
  2336  
  2337      OPM is revising Sec.  351.807(e), which concerns agency 
  2338  determinations of eligibility for certification of expected separation. 
  2339  The prior provision referred to appeal to MSPB. Revised Sec.  
  2340  351.807(e) removes that MSPB reference and states that an agency 
  2341  determination of eligibility for certification may not be appealed.
  2342      This change is also conforming in nature. It aligns Sec.  
  2343  351.807(e) with revised subpart I and clarifies that certification 
  2344  determinations under Sec.  351.807 are not independently appealable 
  2345  under part 351. Employees who are actually furloughed for more than 30 
  2346  days, separated, or demoted by RIF action may pursue any appeal 
  2347  available under revised Sec.  351.901.
  2348  
  2349  C. Subpart I--Appeals
  2350  
  2351      OPM is revising subpart I of part 351 in full. Revised subpart I 
  2352  establishes the procedures governing appeals to OPM by employees who 
  2353  are subject to covered RIF actions. The revised subpart identifies who 
  2354  may appeal, the burden of proof, filing requirements, party 
  2355  submissions, representation rules, adjudication procedures, remedies, 
  2356  sanctions, reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  2357  1. Section 351.901--Right To Appeal
  2358      Revised Sec.  351.901 establishes the right to appeal a covered 
  2359  reduction-in-force action to OPM, identifies the appellant's burden of 
  2360  proof, and defines the relationship between the OPM RIF appeal process 
  2361  and other remedial forums.
  2362      Paragraph (a) provides that an employee who has been furloughed for 
  2363  more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a reduction-in-force action 
  2364  taken under part 351 may appeal that action to OPM. This paragraph 
  2365  identifies the covered actions that may be appealed under subpart I and 
  2366  implements the rule's central procedural change: OPM, rather than MSPB, 
  2367  will adjudicate appeals of covered RIF actions, subject to the 
  2368  applicability provision described below.
  2369      Paragraph (b) establishes the employee's burden of proof. The 
  2370  appellant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the 
  2371  written appeal was timely and in the required form; that OPM has 
  2372  jurisdiction over the appeal; that the agency failed to comply with an 
  2373  applicable statute or OPM regulation governing reduction-in-force 
  2374  actions under part 351; and that the failure prejudiced the appellant.
  2375      Paragraph (b)(4) defines the prejudice requirement. The appellant 
  2376  must show that the agency's failure to comply with an applicable RIF 
  2377  statute or OPM regulation caused the appellant to be subjected to the 
  2378  appealed action or to lose a materially more favorable outcome under 
  2379  part 351. This standard is intended to distinguish prejudicial errors 
  2380  from technical or immaterial errors. OPM will not grant relief solely 
  2381  because an agency committed a procedural or technical error if the 
  2382  appellant would have been subject to the same action, or would not have 
  2383  received a materially more favorable outcome, had the agency complied 
  2384  with the applicable requirement. Conversely, prejudice may exist where 
  2385  the violation affected the appellant's retention standing, order of 
  2386  release, assignment rights, notice rights, or other RIF determination 
  2387  in a way that materially affected the outcome of the RIF action as 
  2388  applied to the appellant.
  2389      Paragraph (c)(1) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  2390  sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action covered by this 
  2391  subpart. This provision is intended to avoid duplicative or overlapping 
  2392  RIF appeal processes and to channel covered RIF appeals through the OPM 
  2393  procedure established by this final rule. It also promotes consistent 
  2394  application of OPM's governmentwide RIF regulations and avoids parallel 
  2395  adjudication of the same RIF-compliance issues in multiple forums.
  2396      Paragraph (c)(2) provides that a reduction-in-force action taken 
  2397  under part 351, and any matter relating to an appeal of such an action, 
  2398  may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested 
  2399  through grievance arbitration. This provision forecloses negotiated 
  2400  grievance procedures and grievance arbitration as alternative forums 
  2401  for direct RIF-compliance challenges, for the reasons discussed in 
  2402  Section III.I of this preamble.
  2403      At the same time, paragraph (c)(3) makes clear that the OPM RIF 
  2404  appeal process does not displace matters within the independent 
  2405  jurisdiction of other entities. Employees may continue to file 
  2406  complaints, appeals, or other matters that fall within the independent 
  2407  jurisdiction of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, an 
  2408  Inspector General, MSPB, the Department of Labor Veterans' Employment 
  2409  and Training Service, or the Office of Special Counsel. Thus, OPM will 
  2410  adjudicate whether the RIF action complied with applicable RIF statutes 
  2411  and OPM regulations, while collateral statutory claims remain available 
  2412  in the forums Congress or applicable law has designated for those 
  2413  claims.
  2414      Paragraph (c)(4) also provides that a party cannot obtain judicial 
  2415  review of a decision under this subpart. OPM addresses comments 
  2416  concerning judicial review and the CSRA remedial scheme in Section 
  2417  III.G.
  2418      Consistent with the DATES section of this preamble, the appeal 
  2419  process established by revised Sec.  351.901 and subpart I is available 
  2420  for a reduction-in-force action for which the agency issued the 
  2421  employee a specific RIF notice under Sec.  351.802 on or after the 
  2422  effective date of the final rule under RIN 3206-AO86. An appeal of a 
  2423  reduction-in-force action for which the agency issued that notice 
  2424  before that date--including an appeal pending before the MSPB--
  2425  continues to be adjudicated by the MSPB under the procedures applicable 
  2426  when the action was taken. This applicability provision is stated in 
  2427  the preamble, and the final regulatory text accordingly does not 
  2428  include a separate applicability note in Sec.  351.901.
  2429  2. Section 351.902--Procedures for Submitting Appeals
  2430      Revised Sec.  351.902 describes the procedures and timeline an 
  2431  employee must adhere to when submitting an appeal.
  2432      Paragraph (a) requires a party, or the party's authorized 
  2433  representative, to file an initial appeal or request for 
  2434  reconsideration through the electronic filing system identified on 
  2435  OPM's website. Unless a party demonstrates good cause and obtains 
  2436  approval from OPM, OPM will not accept pleadings, evidence, or 
  2437  documents submitted by electronic mail or postal mail. This requirement 
  2438  is intended to promote consistent intake, reliable service, accurate 
  2439  case tracking, and efficient adjudication.
  2440      Commenters 0066, 0272, 0296, 0299, 0304, and others, criticized the 
  2441  requirement that employees use e-filing exclusively, absent a showing 
  2442  of good
  2443  
  2444  [[Page 49249]]
  2445  
  2446  cause. OPM disagrees with these criticisms. The good cause requirement 
  2447  permits nonelectronic filing methods for filers with a bona fide need 
  2448  while furthering OPM's legitimate interest in maintaining a streamlined 
  2449  case intake system that minimizes errors and delays. OPM notes that the 
  2450  e-filing requirement for RIF appeals for which this rule provides is 
  2451  consistent with the National Labor Relations Board's policy for 
  2452  requiring parties to e-file documents absent justification to file in 
  2453  paper format.\31\ Other agencies, including the FLRA and OSC, also have 
  2454  adopted restrictions on electronic filing.\32\ OPM acknowledges 
  2455  Commenter 0553's concern that the e-filing system described in the 
  2456  proposed rule was not operational and available for public inspection 
  2457  at the time the proposed rule was submitted for public comment. 
  2458  However, OPM is confident that it will have an e-filing system in place 
  2459  by this final rule's effective date.

  2539  3. Section 351.903--Form and Content of RIF Appeal and Agency Response
  2540      Revised Sec.  351.903 identifies the required contents of the 
  2541  employee's appeal, the agency's response, the agency record, any 
  2542  employee reply, inspection of OPM's appellate record, service 
  2543  requirements, and treatment of untimely filings.
  2544      Paragraph (a) requires the employee's appeal to be in writing and 
  2545  to state the basis for the appeal. The appeal must include the name, 
  2546  address, and email address or telephone number of the appellant and, if 
  2547  applicable, the appellant's representative. The employee must also 
  2548  include any documentation supporting the appeal.
  2549      Paragraph (b) requires the agency to file its response within 30 
  2550  calendar days after service of the initial appeal. The agency response 
  2551  must identify the appellant and the agency whose action is being 
  2552  appealed; identify the reduction-in-force action taken against the 
  2553  appellant and state the reasons for the action; include all documents 
  2554  contained in the agency record of the action; designate and be signed 
  2555  by the authorized agency representative; and include any other 
  2556  documents or responses requested by OPM.
  2557      Paragraph (b) also identifies the minimum contents of the agency 
  2558  record for a RIF appeal. The agency record must include, at a minimum 
  2559  and as applicable, the appellant's specific written RIF notice, any 
  2560  amended notice, proof of service or receipt, and documents showing the 
  2561  effective date of the action. The record must also include documents 
  2562  supporting the agency's stated reason for the RIF, including whether 
  2563  the action was based on lack of work, shortage of funds, insufficient 
  2564  personnel ceiling, reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment or 
  2565  restoration rights.
  2566      The agency record must include documents establishing the 
  2567  appellant's coverage, position, appointment, tenure group and subgroup, 
  2568  veterans' preference status, service computation
  2569  
  2570  [[Page 49250]]
  2571  
  2572  date, work schedule, competitive area, competitive level, and status as 
  2573  a competing employee. It must also include documents establishing the 
  2574  competitive area and competitive level used for the RIF, including any 
  2575  required agency or OPM approval, written competitive-area 
  2576  justification, organizational chart, position descriptions, 
  2577  classification records, representative-rate determinations, and related 
  2578  records.
  2579      In addition, the agency record must include the retention register 
  2580  applicable to the appellant, if one was prepared, and related retention 
  2581  records that affected the appellant's retention standing, order of 
  2582  release, or assignment rights. These records include, as applicable, 
  2583  records supporting performance credit, veterans' preference credit, 
  2584  tenure subgroup, and service computation date. The record must also 
  2585  include documents showing how the agency applied the order of release, 
  2586  including any tie determination, correction of retention standing, and 
  2587  mandatory or discretionary exception to the order of release.
  2588      Where assignment rights are at issue, the agency record must 
  2589  include documents concerning the appellant's assignment rights, 
  2590  including positions considered for assignment, qualification 
  2591  determinations, job analysis or assessment materials, offers of 
  2592  assignment, and any declination. Where a special RIF circumstance is 
  2593  relevant to the appellant, the record must include documents concerning 
  2594  that circumstance, including abolishment of an entire competitive area, 
  2595  transfer of function, exclusion from RIF competition under Sec.  
  2596  351.202(d), restoration protection, or another basis for modified 
  2597  notice or treatment under part 351.
  2598      Finally, paragraph (b) requires a certification that the agency has 
  2599  produced the complete agency record of the RIF action. The final rule 
  2600  distinguishes between production to OPM and service on the appellant. 
  2601  The agency must produce the complete agency record to OPM so that OPM 
  2602  may adjudicate the appeal on the full record relevant to the action 
  2603  under review. The agency must serve the appellant with the agency 
  2604  record, except that the agency may redact or withhold information from 
  2605  the copy served on the appellant to the extent necessary to comply with 
  2606  the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-information or 
  2607  national-security requirements, protective orders issued by OPM, and 
  2608  any other applicable limitation on disclosure required by law. This 
  2609  distinction ensures that OPM receives the full record necessary to 
  2610  decide the appeal while protecting information that may not lawfully be 
  2611  disclosed in full to the appellant or the appellant's representative.

  2637  4. Section 351.904--Employee Representatives
  2638      Revised Sec.  351.904 governs representation in OPM RIF appeals.
  2639      Paragraph (a) provides that an appellant may select a 
  2640  representative of the appellant's choice to assist in preparing and 
  2641  presenting the appeal, provided the employee submits a written 
  2642  designation of representative for the specific appeal. This provision 
  2643  preserves an employee's ability to obtain representation while 
  2644  requiring a clear written designation for the proceeding.
  2645      Paragraph (b) addresses representatives who are Federal employees. 
  2646  If the selected representative is a Federal employee, the 
  2647  representative may not perform representational functions while in a 
  2648  duty status, including while on official time under 5 U.S.C. 7131. The 
  2649  representative also may not claim agency reimbursement for expenses 
  2650  incurred while performing the representational function. This provision 
  2651  limits the use of agency time and resources in connection with RIF 
  2652  appeals under this subpart.
  2653      Paragraph (c) authorizes OPM or the responsible agency to disallow 
  2654  a representative in specified circumstances. OPM or the agency may 
  2655  disallow the employee's choice of representative when the 
  2656  representative is an employee of the responsible agency or OPM and the 
  2657  representative's activities would cause a conflict of interest or 
  2658  position. Because paragraph (b) prohibits a Federal employee 
  2659  representative from performing representational functions while in a 
  2660  duty status, the final rule does not adopt the proposed additional 
  2661  grounds for disallowance based on the priority needs of the Government 
  2662  or unreasonable costs to the Government.
  2663  5. Section 351.905--Adjudication of Appeals
  2664      Revised Sec.  351.905 establishes the procedures for adjudicating 
  2665  RIF appeals.
  2666      Paragraph (a) governs appeals by employees of agencies other than 
  2667  OPM. OPM will assign personnel to adjudicate those appeals. Assigned 
  2668  OPM personnel must be insulated from officials who participated 
  2669  personally and substantially in the challenged personnel action or 
  2670  provided case-specific advice concerning that action. OPM adjudicators 
  2671  may not consider material ex parte communications concerning the merits 
  2672  of an appeal. If such a communication occurs, OPM will place a summary 
  2673  of the communication in the record and provide the parties a reasonable 
  2674  opportunity to respond, unless disclosure is prohibited by law.
  2675      Paragraph (a) also establishes assignment restrictions. No OPM 
  2676  employee may be assigned to adjudicate an appeal if the employee has a 
  2677  relationship with the appellant or, during the preceding two years, was 
  2678  an employee of the agency that is a party to the appeal or was subject 
  2679  to an action covered under part 351. When necessary, OPM may assign an 
  2680  administrative law judge to preside over the adjudication of an appeal 
  2681  by a non-OPM employee.
  2682      Paragraph (b) establishes a separate procedure for appeals by OPM 
  2683  employees. OPM will assign an administrative law judge to adjudicate
  2684  
  2685  [[Page 49251]]
  2686  
  2687  an appeal by an OPM employee. The administrative law judge will issue 
  2688  an initial decision. To insulate adjudication of OPM employees' appeals 
  2689  from agency involvement, OPM will not disturb the initial decision in 
  2690  those cases unless a party shows a harmful procedural irregularity 
  2691  before the administrative law judge, a clear error of law, or a 
  2692  material factual error that affected the outcome of the appeal.
  2693      Under this construction, the OPM Director would be proactively 
  2694  exercising restraint in permitting decisions pertaining to OPM 
  2695  employees to lie undisturbed, not delegating his authority to the ALJ. 
  2696  In essence, the OPM Director is regulatorily tying his own hands but 
  2697  can nevertheless choose to regulatorily untie them. This leaves the ALJ 
  2698  as a properly supervised inferior officer, not a principal officer. See 
  2699  United States v. Arthrex, Inc., 594 U.S. 1, 6 (2021) (holding that the 
  2700  Appointments Clause provides that inferior officers may exercise 
  2701  executive power provided they are directed and supervised by a 
  2702  principal officer.).
  2703      Paragraph (b) defines ``harmful procedural irregularity'' as an 
  2704  irregularity in the application of procedures likely to have caused the 
  2705  administrative law judge to reach a conclusion different from the one 
  2706  the judge would have reached in the absence or cure of the 
  2707  irregularity. The assignment of an administrative law judge under 
  2708  paragraphs (a) or (b) does not make 5 U.S.C. 554, 556, or 557 
  2709  applicable to an appeal under part 351, except to the extent those

  2746  6. Section 351.906--Sanctions and Protective Orders
  2747      Revised Sec.  351.906 authorizes OPM to issue protective orders and 
  2748  cease-and-desist directives, and identifies available consequences for 
  2749  noncompliance. OPM stated in the proposed rule that it believes that 
  2750  MSPB procedures, while providing for protective orders, are inadequate 
  2751  to protect Federal employees from threats and harassment.
  2752      Paragraph (a) permits OPM to issue a protective order or cease-and-
  2753  desist directive to protect the integrity of the adjudicatory process, 
  2754  prevent threats, intimidation, targeted harassment, improper witness 
  2755  contact, disclosure of protected personal information, or misuse of 
  2756  nonpublic information obtained through the appeal. OPM may act sua 
  2757  sponte or at the request of a party, either preemptively or at any 
  2758  point in the appeal process.
  2759      A party requesting a protective order or cease-and-desist directive 
  2760  must file the request through the prescribed e-filing procedures and 
  2761  include a statement of reasons supporting the request, along with 
  2762  relevant documentary evidence. Any protective order issued by OPM must 
  2763  be no broader than reasonably necessary and must not restrict lawful 
  2764  communications protected by law.
  2765      Commenters 0442, 0443, 0513, and 1119 objected to section 
  2766  351.906(a) of the proposed rule, asserting the standards under which it 
  2767  permitted OPM to issue cease-and-desist directives were overly broad 
  2768  and vague such that it would chill employees from exercising their 
  2769  First Amendment right to speak publicly about RIF adjudications.
  2770      OPM has considered these comments and is narrowing Sec.  351.906 in 
  2771  the final rule. The final rule does not adopt the broad ``reasonably be 
  2772  foreseen to lead to harassment'' formulation and does not authorize OPM 
  2773  to bar use of any information related to an appeal for any purpose 
  2774  whatsoever. Instead, OPM may issue a protective order or cease-and-
  2775  desist directive only to protect the integrity of the adjudicatory 
  2776  process; prevent threats, intimidation, targeted harassment, improper 
  2777  witness contact, disclosure of protected personal information; or 
  2778  prevent misuse of nonpublic information obtained through the appeal. 
  2779  The final rule also adds two limiting principles. Any protective order 
  2780  must be no broader than reasonably necessary, and any such order must 
  2781  not restrict lawful communications protected by law.
  2782      OPM declines to remove protective-order authority entirely. Because 
  2783  OPM will adjudicate appeals under subpart I of part 351, it must have 
  2784  reasonable procedural tools to protect witnesses, parties, protected 
  2785  personal information, nonpublic appeal materials, and the integrity of 
  2786  the adjudicatory record. OPM also retains authority to act sua sponte 
  2787  or preemptively where necessary, because threats to the process, 
  2788  improper witness contact, or disclosure of protected information may 
  2789  arise before a party files a motion or before harm has fully occurred. 
  2790  That authority is limited to matters connected to an appeal under 
  2791  subpart I of part 351 and to the specific purposes identified in Sec.  
  2792  351.906(a).
  2793      Paragraph (b) identifies consequences for failure to comply with an 
  2794  OPM directive issued under paragraph (a). Except where prohibited by 
  2795  law, OPM may draw inferences against the noncompliant party, prohibit 
  2796  the noncompliant party from introducing evidence or additional evidence 
  2797  or otherwise relying on the record, or eliminate from consideration an 
  2798  appropriate part of the noncompliant party's filings or submissions.
  2799      OPM is additionally specifying in paragraph (c) that any sanction 
  2800  issued under paragraph (b) must be proportionate, causally related to 
  2801  the violation, and no broader than necessary to protect the 
  2802  adjudicatory process.

  2806  7. Section 351.907--Reconsideration of an Initial Decision
  2807      Revised Sec.  351.907 establishes the process for reconsideration 
  2808  of an initial decision.
  2809      Paragraph (a) authorizes OPM, in its sole discretion, to reopen and 
  2810  reconsider an initial decision upon request of either party or on OPM's 
  2811  own initiative. An employee, the employee's representative, or the 
  2812  agency may request reconsideration within 30 calendar days from 
  2813  issuance of the initial decision. The request must be filed in the same 
  2814  manner as an initial appeal.
  2815      Paragraph (b) identifies the grounds on which OPM may grant 
  2816  reconsideration. OPM may grant reconsideration if the initial decision 
  2817  contains erroneous findings of material fact sufficient to warrant a 
  2818  different outcome; if the initial decision is based on an erroneous 
  2819  interpretation of statute or regulation or an erroneous application of 
  2820  law to the facts; if new and material evidence or legal argument is 
  2821  available that, despite the party's due diligence, was not available 
  2822  when the record closed; or if OPM finds good cause to reconsider the 
  2823  appeal.
  2824      When a party alleges legal error, the party must explain how the 
  2825  error affected the outcome of the case. For new evidence, the relevant 
  2826  question is whether the information contained in the documents, not 
  2827  merely the documents themselves, was unavailable despite due diligence 
  2828  when the record closed.
  2829      Paragraph (c) describes OPM's authority in a reopened or reviewed 
  2830  case. OPM may issue a reopened and reconsidered decision that affirms, 
  2831  reverses, modifies, vacates, or otherwise decides the case in whole or 
  2832  in part. OPM may require the parties to submit argument and evidence, 
  2833  take any other action necessary for final disposition of the case, and 
  2834  issue an order with a date for compliance.
  2835      Paragraph (d) provides that there is no further right of 
  2836  administrative appeal from the reopened and reconsidered decision.
  2837  8. Section 351.908--Review by the OPM Director
  2838      Section 351.908 reserves to the OPM Director the authority, in the 
  2839  Director's discretion and sua sponte, to reopen and reconsider any 
  2840  appeal in which OPM has issued a decision that has not yet become 
  2841  final. Once a decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909, Sec.  351.908 
  2842  does not provide a separate mechanism for reopening that decision.
  2843      Many commenters (including 0177, 0395, 0411, 0555, 1020, and 
  2844  others) objected to providing the OPM Director with the authority to 
  2845  reopen and reconsider decisions at his or her direction, sua sponte, 
  2846  contending that it violated due process.
  2847      In response to comments expressing concern that Director review 
  2848  could be too open-ended or could undermine the perceived neutrality of 
  2849  OPM adjudication, OPM has revised Sec.  351.908 to identify 
  2850  nonexclusive considerations that may inform the Director's decision to 
  2851  reopen and reconsider a nonfinal RIF appeal decision. Under the final 
  2852  rule, the Director may act on the Director's own initiative and only 
  2853  before a decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909. In determining 
  2854  whether to exercise that authority, the Director may consider, among 
  2855  other things, whether the decision contains clear legal error, rests on 
  2856  an erroneous finding of material fact, involves an issue of exceptional 
  2857  importance, affects the governmentwide administration of civil service 
  2858  laws, rules, regulations, or OPM policy, conflicts with another OPM 
  2859  decision, or otherwise warrants Director review.
  2860      This revision responds to commenters who objected to Director 
  2861  review as insufficiently cabined, while preserving final agency 
  2862  supervision over important legal, factual, policy, consistency, and 
  2863  governmentwide civil service issues. OPM has retained sua sponte 
  2864  Director review because final agency oversight promotes decisional 
  2865  consistency and accountability within OPM's adjudicatory process. The 
  2866  revision does not create a separate right for parties to request 
  2867  Director review; parties may seek reconsideration under Sec.  351.907. 
  2868  If the Director reopens and reconsiders a decision under Sec.  351.908, 
  2869  the Director may take any action available under Sec.  351.907(c). This 
  2870  structure preserves meaningful principal-officer oversight while 
  2871  clarifying that Director review will occur within the rule's record-
  2872  based adjudicatory framework, including the final rule's agency-record, 
  2873  separation-of-functions, ex parte, reconsideration, and finality 
  2874  provisions.
  2875      OPM declines to eliminate Director review entirely. Director review 
  2876  serves both administrative and constitutional functions. As an 
  2877  administrative matter, it ensures that OPM can correct material legal, 
  2878  factual, or procedural errors before a decision becomes final; resolve 
  2879  recurring or important questions of interpretation; and promote uniform 
  2880  application of part 351 across agencies. That review function is 
  2881  especially important in a governmentwide personnel system, where 
  2882  inconsistent interpretations by subordinate adjudicators could produce 
  2883  uneven appeal rights for similarly situated employees in different 
  2884  agencies. Cf. 5 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3), (5) (vesting the OPM Director 
  2885  with responsibility for securing ``accuracy, uniformity, and justice'' 
  2886  in OPM's functions, directing and supervising OPM employees, and 
  2887  executing, administering, and enforcing civil-service laws and 
  2888  regulations).
  2889      Director review also reinforces the rule's consistency with the 
  2890  Appointments Clause. The Constitution requires principal officers to be 
  2891  appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, 
  2892  while Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers in the 
  2893  President alone, courts of law, or heads of departments. U.S. Const. 
  2894  art. II, Sec.  2, cl. 2. The OPM Director is a presidentially 
  2895  appointed, Senate-confirmed officer. 5 U.S.C. 1102(a). Under the 
  2896  Supreme Court's Appointments Clause precedents, inferior officers must 
  2897  remain subject to direction and supervision by a properly appointed 
  2898  superior officer. Edmond v. United States, 520 U.S. 651, 663-65 (1997). 
  2899  In the adjudicatory context, the Court has treated the availability of 
  2900  review by a superior executive officer as a significant feature 
  2901  distinguishing inferior officers from principal officers. Id. at 665.
  2902      That principle is particularly relevant where subordinate 
  2903  adjudicators exercise significant authority under Federal law. The 
  2904  Supreme Court has held that officials who occupy continuing offices and 
  2905  exercise significant discretion in conducting adjudications may be 
  2906  ``Officers of the United States'' rather than mere employees. See 
  2907  Freytag v. Comm'r, 501 U.S. 868, 881-82 (1991); Lucia v. SEC, 585 U.S. 
  2908  237, 245-51 (2018). The rule preserves supervision by the Director, a 
  2909  principal officer, before OPM's decision becomes final. Consistent with 
  2910  Freytag, Lucia, and related precedents, the Director will appoint, or 
  2911  ratify the appointments of, the OPM personnel assigned to adjudicate 
  2912  appeals under this subpart, ensuring that any adjudicator who exercises 
  2913  significant authority as an inferior officer has been properly 
  2914  appointed.
  2915      The Supreme Court's decision in United States v. Arthrex, 594 U.S. 
  2916  1, 22-23 (2021), confirms the importance of that structure. There, the 
  2917  Court held that administrative patent judges could not constitutionally 
  2918  issue unreviewable final decisions on behalf of the Executive Branch 
  2919  while being appointed only as inferior officers. The constitutional 
  2920  problem was not that subordinate adjudicators participated in deciding 
  2921  cases; it was that their decisions were insulated from review by
  2922  
  2923  [[Page 49253]]
  2924  
  2925  a principal officer. Id. at 25-26. The Court's remedy was to permit 
  2926  discretionary review by the Director of the Patent and Trademark 
  2927  Office, explaining that the Director need not review every decision, 
  2928  but must have authority to review decisions if he chooses. Id. at 27-
  2929  28.
  2930      The appeals process established in this rule follows that model. 
  2931  OPM adjudicators may issue initial decisions, and OPM may reopen and 
  2932  reconsider those decisions on party request or on its own initiative. 
  2933  In addition, the Director may, in his or her discretion, reopen and 
  2934  reconsider any appeal in which OPM has issued a decision that has not 
  2935  yet become final, and a decision issued by the Director is the final 
  2936  decision of OPM. This structure ensures that no subordinate adjudicator 
  2937  has unreviewable authority to bind OPM or the Executive Branch in an 
  2938  appeal under subpart I of part 351.
  2939      OPM does not agree that the possibility of Director review 
  2940  establishes bias or a due-process violation. Agency heads commonly 
  2941  retain final decisional authority within administrative adjudication 
  2942  systems, and the mere availability of final agency review does not show 
  2943  prejudgment, bad faith, or inability to decide a matter fairly.\33\ The 
  2944  Director's review authority applies only before a decision becomes 
  2945  final. It does not permit adjudication outside the regulatory 
  2946  framework, and it does not eliminate the requirement that decisions be 
  2947  based on the record and the governing standards in part 351. In 
  2948  addition, OPM has revised Sec.  351.908 to identify nonexclusive 
  2949  considerations that may inform the Director's decision to reopen and 
  2950  reconsider a nonfinal RIF appeal decision, including whether the 
  2951  decision contains clear legal error, rests on an erroneous finding of 
  2952  material fact, involves an issue of exceptional importance, affects the 
  2953  governmentwide administration of civil service laws, rules, 
  2954  regulations, or OPM policy, conflicts with another OPM decision, or 
  2955  otherwise warrants Director review.
  2956  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2957  
  2958      \33\ See Fogo de Chao (Holdings) Inc. v. U.S. Dep't of Homeland 
  2959  Sec., 769 F.3d 1127, 1148-49 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (declining to find a 
  2960  due process violation where plaintiff did not establish that the 
  2961  individual agency decisionmaker ``ha[d] a closed mind'' and was 
  2962  ``impervious to evidence or argument''); Riggins v. Goodman, 572 
  2963  F.3d 1101, 1115 (10th Cir. 2009) (denying claim of due process 
  2964  violation absent evidence that administrative adjudicators had a 
  2965  pecuniary interest in the case or personal animosity against a 
  2966  party).
  2967  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2968  
  2969      The final rule thus ensures that Director review occurs within a 
  2970  structured adjudicatory process that includes record-based decision-
  2971  making, separation-of-functions protections, ex parte safeguards, 
  2972  reconsideration, and public availability of final merits decisions. 
  2973  Commenters did not identify specific evidence that the OPM Director 
  2974  would prejudge individual RIF appeals or direct outcomes contrary to 
  2975  the record. OPM therefore declines to eliminate Director review.
  2976  9. Section 351.909--Final Decision
  2977      Revised Sec.  351.909 explains when decisions issued under subpart 
  2978  I become final and the effect of finality.
  2979      Paragraph (a) provides that an initial decision becomes OPM's final 
  2980  decision 30 calendar days after issuance unless, before that time, a 
  2981  party timely requests reopening and reconsideration under Sec.  351.907 
  2982  or the Director reopens the decision under Sec.  351.908.
  2983      Paragraph (b) provides that a timely request for reconsideration 
  2984  under Sec.  351.907 suspends finality. If OPM denies or dismisses the 
  2985  request without reopening the initial decision, the initial decision 
  2986  becomes OPM's final decision 30 calendar days after issuance of the 
  2987  denial or dismissal, unless the Director reopens the initial decision 
  2988  under Sec.  351.908 before that time. If OPM grants the request, the 
  2989  reopened and reconsidered decision becomes OPM's final decision 30 
  2990  calendar days after issuance unless the Director reopens that decision 
  2991  under Sec.  351.908 before that time.
  2992      Paragraph (c) provides that an untimely request under Sec.  351.907 
  2993  does not suspend or otherwise affect finality. If OPM accepts and 
  2994  grants an untimely request for good cause, any resulting reopened and 
  2995  reconsidered decision becomes final as provided in paragraph (b).
  2996      Paragraph d) provides that a decision by the Director under Sec.  
  2997  351.908 that disposes of the appeal is OPM's final decision and is 
  2998  effective upon issuance. If the Director remands the appeal or directs 
  2999  further proceedings, any resulting decision becomes final under Sec.  
  3000  351.909.
  3001      Paragraph (e) states that there is no further right of appeal of a 
  3002  final decision of OPM. This provision works together with Sec.  
  3003  351.901(c), which establishes the OPM process as the sole and exclusive 
  3004  means of appealing covered RIF actions under part 351 and provides that 
  3005  a party cannot obtain judicial review of a decision under this subpart.
  3006      As stated above, OPM is limiting judicial review of decisions 
  3007  issued under this subpart to adhere to the CSRA's specific and well-
  3008  defined statutory scheme for judicial review and prevent unnecessarily 
  3009  protracted litigation regarding RIFs. OPM recognizes the status quo 
  3010  that RIF appeals are appealable to the MSPB and then, in turn, to the 
  3011  Federal Circuit. 5 U.S.C. 7701, 7703(b). However, this pathway 
  3012  currently exists because of an OPM regulation, not because the CSRA 
  3013  itself specifically requires it. The detailed discussion above 
  3014  regarding the structure of the CSRA supports both the legal and 
  3015  prudential bases for limiting judicial review in accordance with the 
  3016  comprehensive statutory scheme. OPM believes that there is little added 
  3017  value from the review that an Article III court could provide relative 
  3018  to OPM's adjudicatory venue.
  3019      Paragraph (f) requires OPM to maintain, subject to legal limits, a 
  3020  publicly accessible website containing final decisions issued under 
  3021  this subpart that address a party's claim on the merits. Those legal 
  3022  limits include requirements protecting privacy, privileged information, 
  3023  protected personnel information, law-enforcement-sensitive information, 
  3024  and other information that may not lawfully be disclosed.
  3025      Final merits decisions that are not posted publicly because of such

  1926  employee from filing a complaint, appeal, or other matter within the

  1928  Labor Relations Authority, an Inspector General, Merit Systems

  1945  11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on the 30th calendar day after the

  1834  grievance and arbitration procedures; that RIF matters are not among 
  1835  the matters excluded from negotiated grievance procedures under 5 
  1836  U.S.C. 7121(c); that questions of arbitrability should be resolved 
  1837  through negotiated grievance procedures; and that OPM may not use a 
  1838  governmentwide regulation to eliminate existing collective-bargaining 
  1839  rights or union representation. Other commenters, including 0221, 0584, 
  1840  0587, 0591, and 0621, asserted that the proposal would unlawfully 
  1841  supersede existing CBAs, while commenters 0386 and 1004 requested a 
  1842  clearer legal basis for OPM's position. Commenters 0049, 0092, 0483, 
  1843  and others objected as a policy matter to any prospective limitation on 
  1844  negotiated RIF appeal procedures.
  1845      OPM has considered these comments and has decided to finalize the 
  1846  regulatory text as initially proposed, with some modifications. The 
  1847  final Sec.  351.901(c) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  1848  ``sole and exclusive means'' of appealing a RIF action, and matters 
  1849  relating to such actions may not be raised under a negotiated grievance 
  1850  procedure or contested through grievance arbitration, but employees are 
  1851  not otherwise impeded from filing a complaint, appeal, or other matter 
  1852  within the jurisdiction of the EEOC, an Inspector General, MSPB, DOL 
  1853  VETS, or OSC.
  1854      OPM continues to conclude that a single governmentwide process for 
  1855  direct RIF-compliance appeals is necessary to ensure uniform 
  1856  interpretation and application of part 351. RIF appeals under part 351 
  1857  involve governmentwide rules governing competitive areas, competitive 
  1858  levels, retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, 
  1859  notice, and related requirements. Allowing agencies to create or 
  1860  bargain for parallel direct appeal mechanisms for the same RIF-
  1861  compliance claim would undermine the consistency, finality, and 
  1862  efficiency the final rule is designed to achieve.
  1863      This conclusion is consistent with 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). That 
  1864  provision states that the duty to bargain extends only ``to the extent 
  1865  not inconsistent with any Federal law or any governmentwide rule or 
  1866  regulation,'' and, for matters that are the subject of a rule or 
  1867  regulation, applies only where the rule or regulation is not 
  1868  governmentwide. 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). This final rule is a 
  1869  governmentwide regulation: it applies across agencies to appeals of 
  1870  covered RIF actions under part 351. To that end, it firmly and 
  1871  completely limits the flexibility of agencies to provide processes not 
  1872  contemplated by this rule, including grievance arbitration. See U.S. 
  1873  Dep't of Treasury, I.R.S. v. FLRA, 996 F.2d 1246, 1250 (D.C. Cir. 1993) 
  1874  (IRS) (5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1) ``permits the government to pull a subject 
  1875  out of the bargaining process by issuing a governmentwide rule that 
  1876  creates a regime inconsistent with bargaining,'' including where a 
  1877  regulation ``sets out an exclusive method of resolving any claims''). 
  1878  Accordingly, agencies may not bargain for a claims-channeling process 
  1879  that conflicts with the final rule's designation of part 351 as the 
  1880  sole and exclusive means of directly appealing a RIF action.
  1881      OPM is not persuaded by commenters' argument that 5 U.S.C. 
  1882  7121(a)(1) overrides this conclusion. Section 7121(a)(1) requires CBAs 
  1883  to provide procedures for settlement of grievances, including questions 
  1884  of arbitrability, and makes those procedures the exclusive 
  1885  administrative procedures for grievances that fall within their 
  1886  coverage. But that provision must be read together with section 
  1887  7117(a)(1), which limits the duty to bargain where the matter is 
  1888  inconsistent with Federal law or a governmentwide rule or regulation. 
  1889  The broad definition of ``grievance'' in 5 U.S.C. 7103(a)(9) likewise 
  1890  does not displace section 7117(a)(1). The fact that RIFs are not listed 
  1891  in section 7121(c) does not mean parties may bargain for an alternative 
  1892  direct RIF appeal procedure that conflicts with a governmentwide 
  1893  regulation establishing a single appeal process.
  1894      The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeal's decision in IRS addressed 
  1895  exactly this issue. The court held that a union proposal that would 
  1896  permit grievances over contracting out was non-negotiable as it 
  1897  conflicted with OMB Circular A-76, a government-wide rule that 
  1898  prescribed the exclusive method for resolving disputes over contracting 
  1899  decisions. The court thus held that Circular A-76 prohibited bargaining 
  1900  over conflicting appeals processes. The final Sec.  351.901(c) 
  1901  similarly prohibits creating an alternative RIF appeals process through 
  1902  collective bargaining.
  1903      OPM also disagrees with Commenter 0962's assertion that section 
  1904  7121(a)(1) has primacy over section 7117(a)(1). Sections 7103, 7117, 
  1905  and 7121 are part of the same statutory scheme and must be read 
  1906  together. Section 7121 establishes negotiated grievance procedures for 
  1907  matters properly within a CBA's coverage; section 7117(a)(1) defines 
  1908  the outer boundary of the bargaining obligation where Federal law or a 
  1909  governmentwide regulation has occupied the field. Reading section 7121 
  1910  to require negotiated grievance arbitration of direct RIF appeals 
  1911  notwithstanding section 7117 would effectively nullify section 
  1912  7117(a)(1) for any matter that could be characterized as a grievance. 
  1913  In IRS the D.C. Circuit expressly rejected that statutory construction. 
  1914  OPM accordingly declines to adopt that reading.
  1915      Nor is this final rule merely a restatement of management rights 
  1916  under 5 U.S.C. 7106. Section 7106 preserves agency authority, subject 
  1917  to subsection (b), to determine mission, budget, organization, number 
  1918  of employees, internal security practices, and to lay off and retain 
  1919  employees, while also preserving bargaining over procedures and 
  1920  appropriate arrangements in appropriate circumstances. 5 U.S.C. 
  1921  7106(a), (b). The final rule does not simply repeat those management 
  1922  rights. It establishes a detailed governmentwide appellate process 
  1923  governing who may appeal, the burden of proof, filing deadlines, 
  1924  agency-record production, service, replies, inspection of the appellate 
  1925  record, representation, adjudication, protective orders, 
  1926  reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  1927  
  1928  [[Page 49245]]
  1929  
  1930      For that reason, commenters' reliance on Office of Personnel 
  1931  Management v. FLRA, 864 F.2d 165 (D.C. Cir. 1988), is misplaced. In 
  1932  that case, the court addressed whether a governmentwide regulation that 
  1933  merely restated management rights could displace bargaining 
  1934  obligations. This rule does not merely restate a management right; it 
  1935  creates a specific, comprehensive appeal procedure for covered RIF 
  1936  actions. The final rule is therefore more closely aligned with the 
  1937  principle that a governmentwide rule may establish an exclusive method 
  1938  for resolving a particular category of claims, rather than simply 
  1939  invoking management rights at a high level of generality.
  1940      OPM also considered comments invoking the general purposes of the 
  1941  FSLMRS, including 5 U.S.C. 7101(a)(1), which recognizes that collective 
  1942  bargaining safeguards the public interest, contributes to the effective 
  1943  conduct of public business, and facilitates amicable dispute 
  1944  resolution. OPM does not dispute those principles. But section 7101 
  1945  must be read with the rest of chapter 71, including section 7117(a)(1), 
  1946  and with section 7101(b)'s direction that chapter 71 be interpreted 
  1947  consistently with the requirements of an effective and efficient 
  1948  Government. Those provisions support, rather than preclude, a 
  1949  governmentwide rule establishing one uniform process for direct RIF-
  1950  compliance appeals and prohibiting grievances over matters pertaining 
  1951  to RIF appeals.
  1952      In addition to the benefits of maintaining a uniform process for 
  1953  direct RIF-compliance appeals, OPM believes it is beneficial to 
  1954  foreclose grievance arbitration in particular as a forum for 
  1955  adjudicating RIF appeals. As OPM explained in the proposed rule, the 
  1956  arbitrators who adjudicate Federal-sector grievances are private 
  1957  contractors who typically do not have a background in agency operations 
  1958  or Federal employment law. This makes them ill-suited to evaluate 
  1959  potentially complex issues involved in arbitration appeals. OPM is 
  1960  aware of multiple studies showing that, across multiple 
  1961  administrations, the FLRA overturns arbitral awards at a high rate.\24\ 
  1962  The author of one of these studies, himself an arbitrator, concluded 
  1963  that ``Federal sector arbitration is more complex than private sector 
  1964  arbitration. The federal field is full of land mines in the form of 
  1965  laws with which federal sector arbitrators may be less familiar.'' \25\ 
  1966  Foreclosing grievance arbitration ensures adjudication will be handled 
  1967  by MSAC employees with specialized legal and subject matter expertise 
  1968  who are less likely to make reversible errors.
  1969  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1970  
  1971      \24\ See James Sherk, ``Federal Union Arbitrators Frequently 
  1972  Misapply the Law,'' (Aug. 2, 2023), https://www.americafirstpolicy.com/issues/expert-insight-federal-union-arbitrators-frequently-misapply-the-law (finding that between 2019 
  1973  and 2023 over 40 percent of arbitration awards were overturned or 
  1974  remanded upon appeal); see also Helburn, B. (2019). The Trump FLRA: 
  1975  Fair or foul (Helburn), at 6. https://cdn.govexec.com/media/gbc/docs/pdfs_edit/060619ew1.pdf (finding the FLRA set aside or remanded 
  1976  arbitration awards 80, 50, and 43 percent of the time in a sampling 
  1977  of cases arising under the Trump 45, Obama, and George W. Bush 
  1978  Administrations, respectively).
  1979      \25\ Helburn at 10.
  1980  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1981  
  1982      Additionally, under 5 U.S.C. 7122(a) arbitral awards concerning RIF 
  1983  appeals are subject to FLRA review. This review can be protracted, 
  1984  especially if the FLRA loses a quorum or the FLRA has a vacancy and the 
  1985  remaining members deadlock.\26\ Authorizing grievance arbitration over 
  1986  RIF actions would thus create a protracted second level of appeals that 
  1987  would undermine the expeditious resolution of cases. OPM declines to 
  1988  adopt this approach.
  1989  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1990  
  1991      \26\ The FLRA has reported that in FY 2024 the average age of 
  1992  pending (not decided) arbitration cases undergoing review was 307 
  1993  days. See U.S. Federal Labor Relations Authority, Congressional 
  1994  Budget Justification 2026, at 19. https://www.flra.gov/system/files/webfm/FLRA%20Agency-wide/Public%20Affairs/CBJ/FLRA%20FY26%20CBJ%20-%20Final.pdf.
  1995  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1996  
  1997      OPM also clarifies that the final rule does not retroactively 
  1998  invalidate existing CBAs or purport to adjudicate particular CBA 
  1999  disputes in this rulemaking. To the extent commenters argued that the 
  2000  proposal would automatically vitiate existing agreements mid-term, OPM 
  2001  does not adopt that position in the final rule. Rather, when agreements 
  2002  are renegotiated, this governmentwide rule will limit agencies' duty 
  2003  and ability to bargain for provisions that create a direct RIF appeal 
  2004  process inconsistent with part 351. Questions concerning the effect of 
  2005  particular existing agreement provisions, negotiability disputes, or 
  2006  unfair-labor-practice allegations remain matters for resolution under 
  2007  chapter 71 by the appropriate forum.
  2008      OPM also disagrees that the final rule eliminates union 
  2009  representation. Final Sec.  351.904(a) provides that an appellant may 
  2010  select a representative of the appellant's choice to assist in 
  2011  preparing and presenting an appeal, provided the appellant submits a 
  2012  written designation of representative for the specific appeal. That 
  2013  representative may be a union representative where otherwise 
  2014  appropriate. Separate limitations on official time, duty status, and 
  2015  reimbursement for Federal employee representatives are addressed in the 
  2016  representation and official-time discussion.
  2017      OPM therefore declines to revise the final rule to permit 
  2018  negotiated grievance arbitration to serve as an alternative direct 
  2019  appeal mechanism for covered RIF actions under part 351. The final rule 
  2020  establishes a uniform OPM process for direct RIF appeals while 
  2021  preserving collateral statutory matters in the forums Congress or 
  2022  applicable law has designated. This approach gives effect to both the 
  2023  RIF appeal framework in part 351 and the limits on bargaining imposed 
  2024  by 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1), while avoiding retroactive invalidation of 
  2025  existing CBAs in this rulemaking.
  2026

[2026-15666: lines 1579-1748 of 4700, FR page 49242]
  1579  G. Judicial Review and CSRA Exclusivity
  1580  
  1581      Many commenters, including but not limited to 0033, 0046, 0114, 
  1582  0308, 0386, and others, criticized the proposed rule's foreclosure of 
  1583  judicial review for RIF appeals adjudicated under the amended 5 CFR 
  1584  part 351. Commenters 0033, 0908, and 1114 asserted that the APA 
  1585  requires OPM to maintain judicial review of RIF appeals, while 
  1586  Commenter 0343 argued that OPM barring judicial review would be an 
  1587  ultra vires action. Commenters 0370, 0928, 1025, 1089, 1092, 1099, and 
  1588  1165 argued that OPM cannot eliminate judicial review by regulation, 
  1589  that judicial review is constitutionally required, that APA review 
  1590  should remain available, and that Federal Circuit review of MSPB 
  1591  decisions has long served as an important external check on RIF 
  1592  adjudication.
  1593      OPM disagrees that the final rule eliminates judicial review that 
  1594  Congress provided. The prior Federal Circuit review path for non-SES 
  1595  RIF appeals depended on two things: OPM's regulation making RIF actions 
  1596  appealable to MSPB and the statutory provisions governing judicial 
  1597  review of MSPB decisions. Once OPM revises its regulation and no longer 
  1598  provides MSPB as the forum for non-SES RIF appeals, the MSPB-to-
  1599  Federal-Circuit review path no longer applies.
  1600      Congress did not provide a separate statutory judicial-review route 
  1601  for non-SES RIF appeals under 5 U.S.C. 3502. The CSRA and related title 
  1602  5 provisions establish a comprehensive remedial scheme for Federal 
  1603  personnel matters, ``prescrib[ing] in great detail the protections and 
  1604  remedies applicable to such action[s], including the availability of 
  1605  judicial review.'' Fausto, 484 U.S. at 443; see also Margolin v. Nat'l 
  1606  Ass'n of Immigr. Judges, No. 25-767, slip op. at 1-3 (U.S. May 26, 
  1607  2026) (Thomas, J., concurring). Where Congress provides review, it does 
  1608  so expressly. Where Congress does not provide a judicial-review route 
  1609  for a particular personnel matter, employees may not use the APA to 
  1610  create an alternative route for challenging that personnel action. See 
  1611  Filebark v. U.S. Dep't of Transp., 555 F.3d 1009 (D.C. Cir. 2009), 
  1612  cert. denied, 558 U.S. 1007 (2009); Fornaro v. James, 416 F.3d 63, 66-
  1613  67 (D.C. Cir. 2005); Graham v. Ashcroft, 358 F.3d 931, 933-35 (D.C. 
  1614  Cir. 2004); Carducci v. Regan, 714 F.2d 171, 172 (D.C. Cir. 1983).
  1615      The CSRA prescribes in precise detail the types of actions that 
  1616  result in eventual judicial review, and it does not provide for such 
  1617  review of non-SES RIFs. 5 U.S.C. 3595(c). Under the CSRA, ``[t]he 
  1618  reviewable agency actions are removal, suspension for more than 14 
  1619  days, reduction in grade or pay, or furlough for 30 days or less.'' 
  1620  Elgin v. Dep't of the Treasury, 567 U.S. 1, 5-6 (2012). Courts have 
  1621  repeatedly dismissed actions brought outside the proper CSRA channels 
  1622  (such as under the APA) by individuals regarding their employment under 
  1623  the comprehensive statutory scheme provided for in the CSRA. See, e.g., 
  1624  Bush v. Lucas, 462 U.S. 367, 368 (1983); Zummer v. Sallet, 37 F.4th 996 
  1625  (5th Cir. 2022); Dotson v. Griesa, 398 F.3d 156, 163 (2d Cir. 2005).
  1626      What is given by the comprehensive statutory scheme in the way of 
  1627  RIF procedures are codified at 5 U.S.C. 3501-3504. While those statutes 
  1628  technically predate the CSRA's enactment in 1978, it has long been 
  1629  recognized that the statutes and regulations regarding reductions-in-
  1630  force in the Federal Government are part of the ``comprehensive 
  1631  employment scheme'' created by the CSRA.\21\ While RIF separations can 
  1632  result in job loss or reassignment, they are specifically excluded as 
  1633  adverse actions under Chapter 75 of Title 5, U.S. Code, which governs 
  1634  removals and discipline for misconduct and, in some cases, performance 
  1635  deficiencies. See 5 U.S.C. 7512(B) (``This subchapter . . . does not 
  1636  apply to . . . a reduction in force action under [Sec.  ] 3502 of this 
  1637  title.'').
  1638  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1639  
  1640      \21\ Filebark v. U.S. Dep't of Transp., 555 F.3d 1009, 1010 
  1641  (Fed. Cir. 2009); see also Nat'l Treasury Emps. Union v. Vought, 149 
  1642  F.4th 762, 774-75 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (applying CSRA claims-channeling 
  1643  in a lawsuit challenging, inter alia, reductions in force); Nat'l 
  1644  Treasury Emps. Union v. Trump, 770 F. Supp. 3d 1, 11 (D.D.C. 2025) 
  1645  (same); Gober v. Collins, No. 25-cv-714 (RC), 2025 WL 1360434, at *6 
  1646  (D.D.C. May 8, 2025) (same).
  1647  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1648  
  1649      ``A RIF is an administrative procedure by which agencies eliminate 
  1650  jobs and account for employees who occupied abolished positions. It is 
  1651  not an adverse action against a particular employee, but it is directed 
  1652  solely at a position within an agency.'' Huber v. Merit Systems 
  1653  Protection Bd., 793 F.2d 284, 286 (Fed. Cir. 1986). ``Unlike adverse 
  1654  actions, RIFs are not aimed at removing particular individuals; rather 
  1655  they are directed solely at positions.'' Grier v. Dep't of Health & 
  1656  Human Servs., 750 F.2d 944, 945 (Fed. Cir. 1984). MSPB concurs, noting 
  1657  the Board's authority ``is not plenary,'' but rather ``the scope of the 
  1658  Board's jurisdiction to review an agency's RIF actions [are] under 
  1659  OPM's regulations at 5 CFR part 351,'' which do not implement Chapter 
  1660  75. Adams v. Dep't of Defense, 96 M.S.P.R. 325, 329 (2004).
  1661      The final rule therefore provides that a party cannot obtain 
  1662  judicial review of a decision under part 351. That provision governs 
  1663  decisions issued under the regulatory RIF appeal process established by 
  1664  this rule. It does not displace collateral statutory claims that 
  1665  Congress has assigned to other forums or that carry their own review 
  1666  provisions. Final Sec.  351.901(c) expressly preserves matters within 
  1667  the jurisdiction of the EEOC, Inspectors General, MSPB where it has 
  1668  independent jurisdiction, DOL VETS, and OSC.
  1669      OPM also disagrees that due process requires Article III review of 
  1670  every RIF appeal. A RIF is a position-based workforce action governed 
  1671  by part 351, not a disciplinary or performance-based adverse action 
  1672  under chapter 75. The final rule preserves notice, a written appeal, 
  1673  production of the agency record, service on the appellant subject only 
  1674  to legally required disclosure limits, a reply, inspection of OPM's 
  1675  appellate record, additional fact development where warranted, hearings 
  1676  when necessary and efficient, written decisions, reconsideration, and 
  1677  corrective relief. OPM concludes that these procedures provide 
  1678  meaningful administrative review for the regulatory RIF appeal right 
  1679  established under part 351.
  1680      Commenters 0033 and 0846 argue that Congress has not spoken clearly 
  1681  on judicial review of RIF appeals. OPM disagrees. The statutory scheme 
  1682  speaks through both text and structure.
  1683  
  1684  [[Page 49243]]
  1685  
  1686  Congress expressly excluded ``a reduction-in-force action under section 
  1687  3502'' from the chapter 75 adverse-action provisions, 5 U.S.C. 7512(B), 
  1688  and the chapter 75 MSPB appeal right applies only to actions covered by 
  1689  that subchapter. See 5 U.S.C. 7513(d). Chapter 77 likewise does not 
  1690  independently create a statutory RIF appeal right; it provides 
  1691  procedures for matters otherwise ``appealable to the Board under any 
  1692  law, rule, or regulation.'' 5 U.S.C. 7701(a). Judicial review under 5 
  1693  U.S.C. 7703(a)(1), in turn, attaches to a ``final order or decision'' 
  1694  of MSPB. Once OPM withdraws the regulatory delegation that made non-SES 
  1695  RIF actions appealable to MSPB, there is no MSPB decision for judicial 
  1696  review under section 7703. Commenters identify no provision in 5 U.S.C. 
  1697  3501 through 3504, chapter 75, chapter 77, or any other Federal 
  1698  employment statute that creates judicial review for non-SES RIF appeals 
  1699  under section 3502. The omission is significant. As the Supreme Court 
  1700  explained in Fausto, Congress's failure to provide review in the CSRA 
  1701  is not a statutory accident but reflects ``a considered congressional 
  1702  judgment.'' 484 U.S. at 448. Congress also demonstrated that it knows 
  1703  how to provide MSPB review of RIF-related actions when it chooses to do 
  1704  so, as it did for certain SES RIF actions. See 5 U.S.C. 3595(c). It did 
  1705  not enact comparable language for non-SES RIF actions under section 
  1706  3502. This omission is significant. It is a basic canon of statutory 
  1707  construction that if ``Congress includes particular language in one 
  1708  section of a statute but omits it in another section of the same Act, 
  1709  it is generally presumed that Congress acts intentionally and purposely 
  1710  in the disparate inclusion or exclusion.'' \22\
  1711  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1712  
  1713      \22\ INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. 421, 432 (1987).
  1714  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1715  
  1716      Commenter 0343 argued that OPM cannot preclude judicial review by 
  1717  regulation. The final rule does not withdraw judicial review that 
  1718  Congress provided; it reflects the review scheme Congress enacted. The 
  1719  prior route to Federal Circuit review existed only because OPM's 
  1720  regulation made non-SES RIF actions appealable to MSPB, and section 
  1721  7703 then provided review of final MSPB decisions. OPM may revise that 
  1722  regulatory delegation through notice-and-comment rulemaking. Nor does 
  1723  the APA supply an independent route around the CSRA. The APA does not 
  1724  apply where ``statutes preclude judicial review,'' 5 U.S.C. 701(a)(1), 
  1725  and courts have repeatedly held that the CSRA is the exclusive remedial 
  1726  scheme for Federal personnel disputes, even where the CSRA provides 
  1727  limited or no relief.\23\ Accordingly, there is no statutory basis for 
  1728  extending judicial review to OPM decisions in non-SES RIF appeals under 
  1729  part 351. OPM's regulations stating that judicial review of RIF actions 
  1730  is unavailable informs the public of the operative legal parameters. 
  1731  Judicial review would be equally unavailable if the final rule said 
  1732  nothing on the subject.
  1733  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1734  
  1735      \23\ See Elgin v. Dep't of Treasury, 567 U.S. 1, 11-12 (2012); 
  1736  Grosdidier v. Chair. of Broad. Bd. of Governors, 560 F.3d 495, 497 
  1737  (D.C. Cir. 2009); Filebark v. Dep't of Transp., 555 F.3d 1009, 1010 
  1738  (D.C. Cir. 2009); Graham v. Ashcroft, 358 F.3d 931, 935 (D.C. Cir. 
  1739  2004); Fornaro v. James, 416 F.3d 63, 67 (D.C. Cir. 2005).

  1747  civil-rights enforcement, eliminate mixed-case processing, prevent

(a) Today 2026-11-14: 351.806 as in effect before 2026-11-18 is not printed in full in task documents; Admin Leave preamble describes it as duty status 'when possible' during notice period, with longstanding emergency paragraph (now (c)) for lack of work/funds. Adopted not yet in force: 2026-21320, 91 FR 65924, published 2026-10-19, eff. 2026-11-18, revises 351.806 to (a) under ordinary circumstances remain in duty status, (b) agency may place on administrative leave for all/part of notice period when appropriate and consistent with part 630 subpart N, (c) emergency lack work/funds annual leave with/without consent, LWOP with consent, nonpay without consent.
(b) Adopted (b) requires agency determination of appropriateness/consistency, no employee consent stated; companion 630.1403(c)(10) at 65940: agency at sole/exclusive discretion, when in Government's best interests, during period between RIF notice and separation. No fixed day limit in (b)/(c)(10) beyond notice period itself; 630.1403(a)(3) usually 1 workday but (c) circumstances may approve more, and (c)(10) is such a circumstance.
(c) OPM says policy already allowed it: Agency Policy Template CPM 2025-12 (2025-07-30) and Fact Sheet already provided authorized official may provide administrative leave between receipt of notice of involuntary separation and effective date; final rule codifies/clarifies existing policy, 65925-65926, 65928-65930.
(d) No change stated: Admin Leave preamble 65925-65926 says rule does not waive/suspend/displace part 351, registers/standing/vet preference continue in full. Standing is fixed as of receipt of notice under 351.507; documents do not provide that leave alters notice or appeal rights.

Head-designee approval under (b)(1) is not OPM approval. 2 In order: career-conditional serving initial probationary period is not competing employee, 351.202(d)(2)(ii); agency may retain while releasing competing, (d)(3). 3 Noncompliant: supervisory probationary period is not initial probationary period, 351.203 definition excludes subpart I supervisory probation; career employee is subgroup I competing, 351.502(a)(2), preamble 49191. Must be ranked. 4 Noncompliant: cutoff 30 days before Oct 13 = Sep 13; 351.503(c)(2) no ratings put on record/used after cutoff, credit based on 4yr prior to cutoff, uniformly applied (c)(4). Oct 2 rating must be excluded for all. 5 Noncompliant: two ratings proxy is average, 351.503(f)(2): (7+5)/2=6, total 18, not presumed L3=15. 6 Noncompliant: additional points only under 351.503(d) for highest level 3 systems or (e) multiple patterns with documented exceptional performance and advance criteria; here single five-level pattern, so no QSI add-on for all. 7 In order: identical total, subgroup, SCD tied for release, agency may select any, 351.601(c). 8 Noncompliant: 351.602 may not release competing employee while retaining employee with specifically limited temporary/term promotion; Reyes temporary promotion ending Mar 2027 bars release. 9 In order: 351.702(a)(4)(v) no assessment required if in 5yr ending on receipt of notice held same position/same grade-pay substantially same duties etc and Level 3+; Silva held same position until 2023 and L4 in 2022 within period ending 2026-10-13. 10 Noncompliant: assessment must allow demonstration, be job-analysis based, not consist solely/principally of automated self-assessment, 351.702(a)(4)(i)-(iii); automated self-rating questionnaire fails, must use acceptable assessment unless (v) applies. 11 Noncompliant: 351.608(a)(3) exceptions stand alone, may not be sequenced/stacked; may apply longest single exception (e.g. 351.608(b) undue interruption max 90 days), not 60+60. 12 Noncompliant: appeal is to OPM not MSPB, within 30 calendar days from effective date with counting/weekend rule, via OPM e-filing, notice must state that under 351.802(a)(6) as revised by appeals rule and 351.902(b); MSPB retains only Foreign Service RIF etc.

(d)(3) proposed may act without regard to part vs final without determining standing under D/E, order of release F, or assignment G, provided consistent with appointment/law; final adds (d)(4) modified notice for excluded employees released for 351.201(a)(2) reasons, content 351.802(a)(1),(3),(5),(6),(b), not (a)(2),(a)(4). 351.203: final adds Restoration protected employee definition; Furlough final omits proposed clause dependent entirely on congressional action; Rating of record proposed pattern in 430.208(d) assessing performance vs final pattern in 430.208(e) for performance of duties. 351.204: final adds administered consistent with all applicable laws including 2301(b) merit principles. 351.302(d): proposed part 752 only vs final 5 CFR part 752 if applicable or other procedures required by law/regulation/appointment. 351.402: proposed only (b); final adds (c) establish/materially modify within 90 days before issuing specific notices - submit description and bona fide basis to OPM for approval in advance, make readily available. 351.502: proposed as of date agency issues specific notice vs final as of date employee receives specific notice; subgroup II competitive proposed temporary or time-limited under C or D part 316 vs final temporary only under D. 351.503(a)(1): proposed 430.208(d), Level 2 Minimally Successful vs final 430.208(e), Minimally Satisfactory; (b)(2) proposed in accordance with 351.501 vs final (corrected) paragraph (a) of this section; (d)/(e)(2) final adds authorized under 430.208(d) prior to 91 FR 41521 qualifier. 351.504(a): proposed should be identified AD/A/B vs final must be identified. 351.505(b)(2): proposed covered by 351.503(b) vs final covered by 351.504(b). 351.506(c)(1): proposed their performance credit/SCDs (all employees) vs final employee's (released employee only); (c)(2) proposed 351.701(b) and (c) vs final (corrected) 351.701(b) only; (d) final adds does not limit access under another statute/regulation. 351.604: proposed revises (b) and removes (d) on furlough criteria; final does not amend 351.604. 351.605: proposed single (a)-(b) vs final restructured (a) use, (b) abolishment plus must provide 351.606 exceptions and may provide 351.608(c)-(f) without 351.608(a)(4) notice, (c) notice identifying area, not ranked, not (a)(2),(a)(4), (d) no register/assignment. 351.606(a): proposed one sentence retention priorities under 351.209(b) vs final (1)-(6) mandatory exception, first determine ordinary standing, may not release if another may be released, reassign if none, OPM placement if agency abolished, no alteration of standing, documentation. 351.608(a)(2): proposed CTAP part 330 subpart E vs final subpart F. 351.701(a): proposed Level 2 minimally successful vs final minimally satisfactory; 351.702(a)(4)(iii) proposed does not solely include/principally rely on self-assessment from automated examination vs final does not consist solely of, or principally rely on, automated self-assessment; final adds (a)(4)(v) no assessment required if in 5 years ending on receipt of notice held same/same grade-pay substantially same duties/series/qualifications/conditions and Level 3 or higher. 351.802(a)(2): proposed veteran status vs final veterans' preference subgroup. Final adds 351.805(b): amended notice solely for later effective date is not new specific notice for 351.507, no redetermination of standing.

Q7.answer:
(a) MSPB hears. Notice 2026-08-31 is before 2026-09-02, so OPM appeals rule does not apply; MSPB continues to adjudicate RIF appeals where notice issued before effective date. Documents bearing: 2026-15665 main rule DATES (notice before = earlier regulations), 2026-15666 appeals rule DATES (applies only notice on/after 2026-09-02), 2026-17338 appeals correction (same eff. date/trigger), 2026-16456 MSPB rule DATES and B (continues RIF appeals, accepts where notice before), 2026-17335 main correction (eff. 2026-09-02, authority/cross-references, does not change trigger).
(b) OPM hears (notice 2026-10-19 on/after 2026-09-02). File through OPM electronic filing system identified on OPM website, unless good cause and OPM approval for other method; not email/postal. 351.902(a). Deadline: 30 calendar days from effective date 2026-12-18, first day counted is day after, 351.902(b)(1): Dec 19 day1 ... Dec 31 day13, Jan 17 2027 day30. Jan 17 2027 is Sunday, so period includes first workday after: Jan 18 2027, by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time under 351.902(b). If Jan 18 is a federal holiday, first workday would be Jan 19 - documents do not list holidays.
(c) Prove by preponderance 351.901(b): timeliness, OPM jurisdiction, agency failed to comply with applicable statute or OPM regulation governing RIF under part 351, and prejudice (caused appealed action or loss of materially more favorable outcome). No hearing as of right: review based solely on written record unless OPM determines hearing necessary and efficient (record insufficient on material fact or material witness credibility dispute), 351.905(c).
(d) Rule: 351.901(c)(2) RIF action/matter relating to appeal may not be raised under negotiated grievance procedure or contested through grievance arbitration; (c)(1) as corrected sole/exclusive in this subpart. Preamble 49244-49245: does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs; when renegotiated, governmentwide rule limits duty/ability to bargain for inconsistent direct RIF appeal process; effect of existing provisions/negotiability/ULP remain for chapter 71 forum.
(e) No. 351.901(c)(4): party cannot obtain judicial review of decision under subpart; 351.909(e) no further appeal of final decision. Collateral claims in preserved forums are distinct.
(f) Yes, potentially under tolling 351.902(b)(3): collateral complaint timely filed before filing period expired with OSC (entity in 351.901(c)(3)), final decision materially affects retention standing (OPM in sole discretion determines materiality; correction would have changed standing), may file within 30 calendar days after decision becomes final/no longer subject to further administrative review. Final decision 2027-03-10: day1 Mar 11, day30 Apr 9 2027, by 11:59 p.m. ET via e-filing, subject to OPM materiality determination.
(g) Appeals rule DATES at 49230: applies only to RIF action for which agency issues specific RIF notice under 351.802 on/after 2026-09-02.
